---
title: "Example: how much a trip by public transport varies"
description: >
  Percentiles of the travel time on a frequency-based network, and one trip
  split into walking, waiting and riding, departure by departure.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("setup.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 5, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
```

By car or on foot, a trip takes the same time whenever it starts. By public
transport it does not: it depends on when the next vehicle leaves. This
example measures that variation in two ways, with percentiles over a window
of departures, and trip by trip. Everything below is one script; the output
shown is the output it prints.

```{r}
library(peabiru)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Percentiles on a frequency-based network

The São Paulo sample that ships with the package has a feed described by
frequencies ("a bus every 8 minutes") rather than timetables. For such
routes peabiru draws random schedules consistent with the frequencies, 5 per
departure minute by default, so the travel times of a window of departures
form a distribution. `seed` makes the draws reproducible.

```{r spo}
spo <- system.file("extdata/spo", package = "peabiru")
network <- build_network(spo)
points <- read.csv(file.path(spo, "spo_points.csv"))
departure <- as.POSIXct("2019-05-13 14:00:00", tz = "America/Sao_Paulo")

ttm <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points[1, ], points[-1, ],
  mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure,
  time_window = 60,
  percentiles = c(5, 25, 50, 75, 95),
  seed = 42
)
ttm <- ttm[order(ttm$travel_time_p50, ttm$travel_time_p95), ]
head(ttm)
```

The destinations closest to the origin are walked to, and every departure
takes the same time. Further away, a bus or the metro saves time, and the
spread between the 5th and 95th percentiles is the price of not knowing when
it comes:

```{r spread, fig.alt = "Range bars of the travel time from one point in São Paulo to 26 others, sorted by median: the nearest destinations have no spread; those reached by bus or metro spread by up to about ten minutes between the 5th and 95th percentiles."}
ttm$destination <- factor(ttm$to_id, levels = rev(ttm$to_id))
ggplot(ttm, aes(y = destination)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = travel_time_p05, xmax = travel_time_p95),
                 colour = "#c98a1d", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = travel_time_p25, xmax = travel_time_p75),
                 colour = "#b4532a", linewidth = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = travel_time_p50), shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Travel time (minutes)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

## Trip by trip

`expanded_travel_time_matrix()` keeps one row per departure minute (and per
draw, on a frequency-based network) instead of percentiles. With
`breakdown = TRUE`, each trip is split into its parts, and the routes taken
are listed. Here, from Farroupilha Park to the PUCRS university campus in
Porto Alegre, whose sample (from r5r 2.5.0) has bus timetables:

```{r poa}
poa <- file.path(tempdir(), "poa")
dir.create(poa, showWarnings = FALSE)
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ipea/r5r/v2.5.0/r-package/inst/extdata/poa/"
for (f in c("poa_osm.pbf", "poa_eptc.zip", "poa_trensurb.zip",
            "poa_points_of_interest.csv")) {
  if (!file.exists(file.path(poa, f))) {
    download.file(paste0(url, f), file.path(poa, f), mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
  }
}
poa_network <- build_network(poa)
poi <- read.csv(file.path(poa, "poa_points_of_interest.csv"))

trips <- expanded_travel_time_matrix(
  poa_network,
  origins = poi[poi$id == "farroupilha_park", ],
  destinations = poi[poi$id == "pucrs", ],
  mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = departure,
  time_window = 30,
  breakdown = TRUE
)
head(trips[, -(1:2)], 10)
```

Leaving at 14:02 or at 14:20 means boarding the same line, but waiting
longer for it; at 14:07 a different pair of buses wins. Stacked bars show
where the minutes go:

```{r breakdown, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Thirty stacked horizontal bars, one per departure minute from 14:00 to 14:29, split into walking to the stop, waiting, riding, transferring and walking from the stop; the totals range from about 30 to 40 minutes, and the waiting time changes most."}
parts <- c(access_time = "Walk to the stop", wait_time = "Wait",
           ride_time = "Ride", transfer_time = "Transfer",
           egress_time = "Walk from the stop")
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(parts), function(p)
  data.frame(departure = substr(trips$departure_time, 1, 5),
             part = factor(parts[[p]], levels = rev(parts)),
             minutes = trips[[p]])))
ggplot(long, aes(minutes, departure, fill = part)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#8db9a0", "#3d4f56", "#b4532a", "#c98a1d", "#2f6b4f"),
                    breaks = unname(parts), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Minutes", y = "Departure") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

## Variations

- **Arrive by.** `arrival_travel_time_matrix()` answers the reverse
  question: the latest departure that arrives by a given time.
- **Fewer transfers.** `max_rides = 1` keeps only the trips with a single
  vehicle; compare the totals.
- **More draws.** `draws_per_minute` sets how many random schedules are
  drawn per minute on frequency-based routes.

The figures on the [home page](../../index.html#gallery) draw the same results
with `site/figures/figures.R` in the repository.
